body: This is an excellent idea which has had measured progress from the first time I visited it in 2003 when Mr Madugalle was the Manager. I knew him as a quiet conscientious person when he was Manager, Thotulagalla Estate, Haputale. He has now retired but left a great legacy on which some great opportunities await.I last visited this place in August 2015 and questioned the ladies there as to whether there had been new developments in the past three years. Sadly, they confirmed that there were no developments so I didn't make the effort to spend more time here.However for the first time visitor it does give a glimpse of the tea manufacture processes of the past and they can make up their minds as to how this place can be made to capture the imagination of a greater number of visitors. The tea industry of Ceylon is in rapid decline because there is a lack of vision for its future. The British gave this country a wonderful legacy upon which a significant future was squandered away. The country has lost its European markets and this industry is mired in practices which are known to most people through their own media in the country as totally inappropriate. The sad thing is that most people who can do something about it lack the energy, courage and ability to do anything about it. Still the Museum as it stands is an effective monument to the creative effort of many good people to provide an opportunity for an outstanding character to take this industry to a better place.It calls for hard work, courage, fortitude and capability to turn it around. The rewards will be substantial but the inheritors have taken a long time-about 45 years.

body: Museum with a relatively small but interesting collection. Very charismatic building (old tea factory). Well maintained. Few visitors only.Take a guide for the ground level exhibits, which are the most interesting. Can buy good priced tea at the 4th floor.

body: So this museum is a very quiet place but well maintained and holds all the traditional machinery used to manufacture tea leaves. Even machines dating back to colonial times. You even get a chance to sample different types of tea.So if you're really interested then go otherwise this place might come across as quiet and boring.

body: We spend a few enjoyable hours here. It is around 4km fro the city centre of Kandy. The ride to the museum is already quite nice as it takes you away from the hustle and bustle of Kandy. The last few 100s of meters you actually pass some tea plantations already to get you in the mood.We did call in advance to make sure they were up and running on a Saturday. Upon arrival it looked like we were the only guests though more people followed. Still not busy anyway. Reading some of the other reviews we sort of expected information not to be readily and easily available. Guides are available, though we did not bother using one nor checking prices. There is a fair bit of information available in the museum but you do need to make the effort to read it. Lots of old stuff including equipment but also newspaper clippings that describe what went on in the old days. Some of it supported by extra boards with information.Nice write ups on how Taylor and Lipton started and expanded their business. The top floor has a sort of summary display that explain the benefits of tea, what happened in the industry as well as the process. It would have made sense to put that first and then go into the details of machines and the process.There is one floor with some shops that sell tea. Interestingly no real hard sales going on there. We went to the Tea Board shop to get some teas as gifts. Good variation and decent prices.Although not all is super clear laid out for one, our visit was enjoyable and we did learn a fair bit about tea and the industry development so worth the visit.We paid just over 600rps entrance fee at 9 august 2014.

body: We visited in July, which isn't really tourist season as it's pretty hot. The museum was very quiet but we learnt a lot about the 2 main tea companies we know, Lipton's and Taylor's. You need to be able to walk up the stairs to the 5 floors of the museum, showing you how a factory would've worked. body: I cant believe we had this place to ourselves, The tea shops are quite cheap and the free tour guide makes this place. Not on the beaten track but its worth the small detour

body: Learned a lot about early tea production and saw excellent machinery. Tour guides available if needed.

body: The Ceylon Tea museum was incorporated on 9th January 1998 under Section 21 of the Companies act no 17 of 1982 and declared open to the public on 1st December, 2001. It is housed in the 1925 established Hanthana tea factory, 4kms from Kandy and at a height of 2499 feet. The museum consists of four floors. The ground floor has the Engine room and Rolling room where old machinery connected with the tea industry are displayed. The first floor has Drier room and furnace room and related machinery displayed. The second floor has sifting room and related equipments. The James Taylor museum and the archive room is also located on this floor. The third floor is allocated to Tea sales outlets where one can buy the finest selection of Ceylon Tea.The entire fourth floor area is a restaurant where visitors are served complimentary tea. They can also take part in Tea tasting session. A panoramic view of the Kandy town surrounded by beautiful Hunnasgiriya Knuckles range and the Matale range of hills can be viewed through a telescope here. This floor also has the original cat walk platform which was used by the superintendent and the tea maker of the tea factory for monthly inspection of the roof and removal of any tea fluff.
title: Must visit museum in Kandy-Revisit the rich tea heritage

body: This is another free of cost tourist attraction which I found very interesting! The staff takes you through all the stages of tea manufacturing starting with the freshly plucked green leaves! Very informative and they wrap up the session with a free cuppa of freshly brewed Sri Lankan tea!
title: interesting and informative

body: The best thing was the journey up to the museum.The tour was fine, but we didn't know the basics about Tea growing/making and she didn't explain any of it to us, and therefore we struggled to understand what she did tell us (3 Doctors, we aren't stupid!)I subsequently went to two different working tea factories and they were miles better, the tour at the others was really informative and seeing the machines working gave a much better idea of what it was all about. At Mackwoods they also take you to a tea bush and explain there which helps.I wouldn't go, go to a working tea factory, there are so many choice of places to explore the tea industry, no need to go to a sub-optimal one.Tour is about 5-10 mins and there are then 3 floors to look around and on the top floor is a cafe for you to have a complimentary taste of tea. 3rd floor is shops but they were mostly closed as we went out of season.
title: Long journey, short tour

body: You need to take transport upto the Tea Museum which sits high up just outside Kandy. The original building is still standing and is quite a few stories high. Each level leads you through some of the history of tea in Sri Lanka and we were fascinated to find out it started with a young 17 year old Englishman sent out to run a coffee plantation. On the top level you can drink some tea and compare the different types. informative and fun.

body: A good place to learn about tea history machinery.They give a free tour, in our case the lady guide was quite knowledgeable.They have tea making machines dated 1880.After the tour they offer a free cup of tea, and then you can buy tea from two tea shops there or some souvenirs from a souvenir shop.

body: Very interesting to see the museum and how tea is made and how the different kinds of teas are produced. Well worth a visit.
title: Very interesting

body: The place is located about 6 km away from Kandy city on Hanthana road. When you move along the Hanthana road, you get the chance of seeing the tea plantations as well. It is open everyday from 8.30 t0 4.30 except on Mondays and Public holidays. Housing of the entire museum is with in an old abandoned tea factory. It has the very first hand operated tea leaf crusher and many more old machines used in the tea industry in the past. It is interesting to note, the special place given for the personal belongings of James Tailor who introduced the tea industry to Sri Lanka. It also gives information about the entire tea processing and gives an idea about the available tea grades. But there should be suitably knowledgeable demonstrators to show the place for the visitors who have no knowledge about the tea processing.
title: A place to learn the history of Sri Lankan tea Industry

body: I have been to tea museum twice, once recently and the staffs were useless. They were doing nothing other than chatting each other. I have been to Loolkondura, the first commercial tea plantation and the James Taylor’s museum also before. Now, everything has been transferred to this location. Why? I was told it was convenient but no use of having any of the displays without a proper guide.It seems everyone in the museum assumes that the people who are coming to this place are tea experts. There is no one to explain the tea processing methodology or how to categories tea as BOP, BOPF etc..I strongly feel that this museum should be used to educate visitors and promote tea by letting people know almost everything about tea. Frankly, it’s a shame to say, this is a useless place unless the management take a U turn soon.

There are 4 floors to the museum and the basic overview of tea production on the upper floor is better than the cut off newspaper clippings on the ground floor.I also visited "Pedro Tea Estate", an active tea factory in Nuwara Eliya, afterwards and feel like that was visit over there was giving me similar, yet a little more lively insights. body: The guided tour gives you a good understanding of how tea is produced after plucking the light green leaves. After the tour in the factory you have the opportunity to have some fresh tea. We enjoyed the tour a lot.

body: this museum is good if you also get to see an old fashioned factory/ plantation. it pulls all of the information together. its still worth visiting if you dont go to both. good selection of machinery and articles. there is not too much to overwhelm you or too little that its not worth going to. 150 rps tuk tuk they may wait if you agree a price, we walked back down. 400rps entrance.

body: The Kandy Tea Museum is a really great insight to how tea is made. 1 ton of drinking tea per 5 tons of leaves...wow. Well worth grabbing some tea to bring home...expecially the blossom - it is worth the money!

body: If you don't like tea this is still a good place to be... If you like tea then this place is awesome!This old tea factory 4km up from Kandy in the hillside now serves as a tea museum with detailed insight as well as quite some real exhibits from the days of good ol' tea production (which is in many ways the same still as today anyway;-)Seeing this place was, for us, only part of some exploration on Sri Lanka's past, it's tea production and all about tea in general, beginner's level, that is... (The other part being at an operational tea estate - in our case Pedro in Nuwara Eliya) What you get to see in the museum will set you right to learn a good deal on the subject and how it had an impact on Sri Lanka on many levels.However, it should be mentioned that the manner in which all is explained and depicted is also a bit of the old-fashioned way. body: our driver took us here and we were well impressed with the guides telling/showing how our tea we drink is processed from field to tea bag well worth a visit

body: Learning about the Scot Lipton and how hard pickers have to work so hard for our cuppa were eyeopeners

body: you visit this place and you get to know the various ways and means in which the superb Sri Lankan tea is made.....We just loved it. we also purchased good amount of tea variety from there.

body: The tea & other purchases were a little expensive compared with market prices but the history if the industry is def' worth checking out. Pity no rolling tea plantations about ;-(
title: Lovely staff, very educational.

body: While the entrance fee seemed high - another attraction designed to make money from tourists - it could be worthy if you are on a tea journey through the country. The museum was empty when we visited and we had a guide to ourselves. The guide was sweet but seemed in a hurry to finish with the tour. I could tell that they don't get many questions as the tea tour was backward! I'd expect the tour to start with the planting of the tea bush, the plucking...leading to the processing and packaging. However the tour started from the last stage of the production process. A bad layout but I suppose most tourists don't care and are interested in just getting through it so they can sit on the top floor cafe and sip their hot cuppa that marks the end of the tour.
title: Lot of history but could be better presented

body: ok, every hill station has a tea museum, so is kandy. Nothing new. They say the entire process of how tea is made, which i believe you would have heard since schooling.
title: similar to other tea museums

body: Situated in Hantana and a lovely place to visit for its uniqueness. The museum consists of historical machinery used in the tea plantations and also a nice library. They also sell tea there for purchase.
title: Rare...

body: We checked on their website and the signs around Kandy that the museum would be open. We negotiated tuktuks for the whole way there and back but when we arrived the museum was closed!I would definitely try and check before going- it is quite a nice drive up through the hills and some tea plantations. We tried to work out the bus but were told by friends that it was really hard to find. Actually we passed a couple of buses in our tuktuk so they seem fairly frequent and stop a short walk from the museum so getting there by bus would be possible.
title: It was closed!

body: You have to be a tea entusiast to find this exiting. Its expensive and boring, you get a Nice cup of tea though.... And unless you go to see the teaplantations the view is the only good Thing to see
title: Not worth it

body: Up the mountain near Kandy a former tea factory has been transformed in the tea museum.The museum explains in great detail the proces of making tea and how Sri Lanka/Ceylon became the great tea-producing country it is now. Absolutely worth a visit if you're interested in tea. Ask the threewheeler for a round-trip, since the museum is located out of town.
title: Knowledgeable guide, lots of tea-history

body: Situated few miles away from Kandy town surrounded with beautiful tea estates. I have been to this place twice with different people and it gives different kind of experience to all of us.Tea Museum is abounded tea factory that has converted to a museum.Can experiance most of the equipment / mechanisms used in creating tea in old days. In the top floor there is a restaurant that you can enjoy a cup of tea of your choice.Locals do have a lower rate while foreigners high, but for the foreign ticket they give some free documents plus free tea to enjoy. There are some shops too that you can buy some tea, but you can find same shop from Colombo too.Do have a walk around the place so you can have nice pictures locations.
title: Unique Experiance

body: We did this as part of an afternoon touring the local sights. We were the only ones there, and got a quick guided tour on how tea is made and the history of tea in Ceylon - we gave the lady a few hundred rupees. It didn't take long and there was a cup of tea at the end. There are numerous bottles of tea leaves on the counter when you get your tea - presumably for smelling? Anyway - you don't get a choice, you get the BOP which was fine. It was a lovely building. They have a section of tea shops at one point - it is a little awkward as it seems that they all have pretty much the same thing, but are run by different ladies - so hard to choose which one to give your business to. Niether of us are tea drinkers, so we just passed.
title: Interesting, worth a stop

body: Building itself is a beautiful example of a typical tea factory, set in a plantation high above Kandy.Remember that this is a museum so expect mechanical relics of a bygone era and all the accessories/equipment and documents associated with tea manufacture.Interesting place and worth a visit if you're in the area, however I wouldn't recommend making a specific visit to Kandy just for this attraction.
title: A Little Lacking

body: There is so much to learn and appreciate from the museum that I will probably go back again. The process of making tea has hardly changed over centuries and it is worth taking time to go to a plantation and also the museum.
title: Fascinating

body: We did this after visiting the Elephant orphanage doesnt take long, doesnt take very long, and cup of tea at the end, would suggest taking plenty of water to drink on any of these trips.
title: Worth a visit if in the area

body: You can't come to Sri Lanka & not visit a tea factory & take home some local tea, even if it does taste just like Tetley!! We had an interesting 30 minute tour & a free brew at the end (but expected to tip the guide). Unfortunately it was a public holiday the day we visited so no idea what is looks & sounds like when working but still an interesting insight into our national drink.
title: Must do trip

body: Wonderful old building, very spacious and open. We walked back down towards Kandy, along the main road. Quite a pleasant walk for most of the way, although there is quite a bit of traffic on the road. The tour of the museum was fine. And the tea tales interesting. Cheap tea to buy and worth the visit.
title: Amazing building

body: We enjoyed very much our walk through this interesting old tea factory. The mixture of old machinery, photographs and memorabilia as well as the building itself meant that there were things of interest for both my wife and myself.
title: Discovering the History of the Cup of Tea

body: We went to the Tea Museum in the morning by tuk tuk. It was an enjoyable ride up the mountain sides to get there. It was practically empty when we went which is a shame. They have it nicely set up and organised and the woman offered to show us around. She was so delightful and was all smiles! It is cool to see all the old machines they used to use and there are some nice artifacts as well. After the tour, they give you a nice cup of tea (try the B.O.P.!) and their small gift shop has really good priced tea as well. If you have time, I recommend this visit, it won't take you more than an hour.
title: Lovely visit!

body: The tour guide was very informative and she gave the tour at no extra cost. Brilliant museum - you get a free cup of tea at the end as well.
title: Interesting

body: After walking around Kandy for a while, I delved into my Rough Guide book for the closest tea factory and came across an entry about this museum. I decided to give it a go! Hardly any of the tuk-tuk drivers knew about it... so make sure you tell them where it is! The museum itself is based in an old tea factory building - which in itself is impressive. The views are breathtaking - a glorious vantage point for the city and the Knuckles mountain range. The exhibits and information seem slightly dated - but still fascinating. On the top floor there is lovely restaurant where you may enjoy a complimentary cup of pure Ceylon tea. There is a shop that sells good quality tea at bargain prices too!! Entry to the museum is 500 rupees for tourists and there are guided tours available. Worth a visit if you're interested or like tea!
title: Lovely little gem, hidden away in the hills

body: I had never been to a tea museum before so I wanted to check this out and I'm glad I did. The bottom few floors are filled with late 19th Century machines used to process the tea, which are impressive. You also get the story of how the Sri Lanka tea industry started with the Brits. On the top floor you get a sample cup of tea in a very nice room with great views. Admission was 500 rupee (US$4) and they offered a guide on a voluntary tips basis. I started without the guide, but then asked for one and am happy I did. She explained the machines and process well, and seemed pleased enough with the 200 rupee tip I gave her (the tour is only about 15 minutes).
title: Not amazing but worth a visit if you are curious about tea

body: I visited the Ceylon Tea Museum this morning after deciding none of the overpriced tuk-tuk excursions sounded remotely tempting - a decision I'd make again and again.The museum is based within a former tea factory and situated amongst beautiful, tea-rich hills overlooking the city. The exhibits are fascinating and quirky, the staff incredibly welcoming and enthusiastic, plus the views increasingly incredible on each storey.I rode up by tuk-tuk (400 rupees, although the driver needed directions from fellow locals) and walked the two or three miles downhill towards Kandy railway station. Probably the best option if, like me, you're able to visit on a scorchingly-hot (32 degrees C!) and sunny day.Great brew in the restaurant, too!
title: Great museum, hidden in the hills

body: The Tea Museum, Hantane, Kandy. The ancient Tea Factory of Hantana Estate is converted into a Museum dedicated to the history of Sri Lankan Tea. Run by the Sri Lanka Tea Board.
title: Visit this place to buy good quality tea!!!

body: The place is not visited much; but I think this is because not many know about it. I loved the walk around the old tea factory and the staff were ever so warm and friendly; more than willing to show us around; and greeting us with smiles all round! The miniature running model of the tea-factory was the high-light! The whole trip was very informative and the end tea was refreshing!
title: Very Informative!

body: If you like old british machinery, a bit of victorian nostalgia or just a rest from the bussle of Kandy for an hour or two this is a nice place. Probably what you have seen before, but old school, with a working model of an old tea factory. Only needs an hour, but it is in the hills near the tea research institute, so tea fields, nice little drive and so quiet. I saw one other person while I was there, the building is beautiful with all old wood panels and fans. They have a few vendors selling different teas on the top floor as well, and an uninspired cafe with great views.
title: Hard to find and nobody goes

body: I hate tea, but I went here with my husband. After holding my nose a lot, I eventually got used to the smell (it is like being in a teapot!). You get to see how tea is manufactured and is quite interesting.
title: I hate tea but I liked the factory

body: A great place where you can see History at work. Even though it celebrates Colonial times seeing the machines of the late industrial revolution at work is fascanating, and at the end you get a great cup of tea
title: Tea Museum

body: if you can find a place in Sri Lanka where they don't just have the machines but also use them, it's more interesting. Also the entrance of 500 roepies is too much. The view over the hills is nice but not just there.
title: not really worth to visit

body: We had a lovely relaxing tour of the tea museum. The lady that conducted our tour was very knowledgeable and also very friendly.
title: A gem

body: We walked all the way up the mountain to get there and the views alone were worth it!!! Not for the faint hearted but well worth it to see the tea plantations and workers picking leaves! The actual museum has some very interesting facts about the commercialism room of tea and its history. Also intrigued to read to read about how people are trained to rate the quality of tea. If you complain about paying $4 entry don't be so cheap! You even get a cup of tea :)
title: Interesting for the tea lovers

body: Very quiet when we visited, but the tour guide was excellent guiding us round the various exhibits. If you're mechanically minded it's particularly interesting. Then at the end of the tour you get your cup of ceylon tea in the 'cafe'.
title: Tour of Tea Museum

body: A good tour from a friendly and informative guide of an old tea factory? Drink tea and shop on the top floor
title: Friendly and interesting

body: We only went as it was raining and it was inside, but it was surprisingly interesting (however we are both English and like our tea...). The museum is set in a beautifully restored tea factory and contains loads of the old machinery, which my engineering husband geeked out over. Some interesting exhibits on James Taylor and Thomas Lipton, the godfathers of tea in Sri Lanka.A tour is included in the price of your entry, as is a cup of tea on the fourth floor. Beautiful views over the surrounding hills.
title: Interesting, beautiful building and setting

body: This museum is a worthy trip from kandy. The winding roads leading up offer some spectacular views over the city. The tea museum features some impressive old machines and shows that early tea production has not changed a bit. The 500rs entry fee could be better spent fixing the private road leading to the estate as it has potholes that could swallow a car.
title: Good old tea museum

body: Super friendly employee showed us different kinds of tea with tasting. It is possible to buy tea afterwards, good as a gift.We were introduced to the art of making tea etc.
title: Do not miss it, very interesting

body: The ticket price is 500rs per person and it's worth it. What you get is a round tour from one of the guides inside (if you want). They will tell you everything about the tea production and how the tea process is working and the history behind it. No question is to hard to answer for them. Lots of pictures on the walls on the upper floors and instruments that was used in the 1800s. Loved it!
title: Interesting historical sight

body: Nicely maintained museum. Would have been good to have a guide. 4 floors of history.Had a small restaurant, but it was closed when we visited
title: Good history

body: If you never went to a tea structure or museum it is worth going. Interesting to hear/see the history of Ceylon tea. The staff is friendly. Too bad you have to pay to get in.
title: ok...but....

body: This is not a working tea factory (once you have seen one of those you have seen them all!) but rather a well presented collection of old equipment and artefacts in an old factory building. We arrived first thing in the morning and were given a well-informed tour of the lower floors by a smartly dressed guide. Although the guide was not allowed to wait whilst we read everything we wanted to, she did indicate that after the tour was over we would be free to wander round at our leisure. After the tour we headed up to the top floor where we had what we rated as the best cup of tea on our entire holiday. On the other hand if you just want to see a noisy 19th century factory filling in time (because the tea processing is done at night) then they are two a penny elsewhere in Sri Lanka. This place is however unique.Do yourself a favour - take a guide to show you round first.
title: Lots of insights into tea making for those with the time to look

body: Sri lanka famous for tea, this museum has great details about tea history in sri lanka, and some equipment which they use to make tea in eariler time. You can buy many tea product from the shop. Tip ; monday's it close
title: Wan't to see how it make

body: It was excellent. But fee is too high for Indian. The staff are very cooperative. Many things to learn about Tea industries. Shopping center of the museum is good
title: Lovely Museum

body: I had big expectations with this museum, but we finished our visit in 15 minutes...not worth to go up the hill this distance. Empty floors...no sigh of any tea drinking possibility but also no sign of much to see. I have not seen one leaf of tea in the whole building...not even provisory...When i asked if it is possible to go to a plantage...i was sent to Front Office to agree...Front office was an another person (beside 3-5 fully bored guids at the entrance) i suppose for an additional fee as we learned in SriLanka...No, it is better to visit a real tea factoy. And by the way...British should have stayed in this country longer...probably some development would have been in investing to new machines last century and the factories would not use the same machines like in the museum...from the 19th century....
title: Empty spaces....

body: This is situated on top of the famous "Hantana" mountain . Old tree factory has been converterd to a museum . Manage by Ceylon tea board . There are three floors here . Fourth floor has a tea canteen . Third floor has tea shops . You can buy from here .other two floors have machines and roller use for tea production. Also have sections of tea research board items and Farther of tea " James Taylor's " items and pictures .. Have to pay a nominal amount to see the place . Good tea borad guide also available to explain the stuff
title: "Only place to see history of Ceylon tea"

body: Maybe im not passionate enough about the tea process. Our guide was fantastic though, very friendly and knowledgeable, wish we could have paid her instead of the museum
title: Expensive for what it was

body: Brilliant! What an interesting museum. Fantastic to see a working museum and have the process from picking to packaging explainednso eloquently. 5 stars.
title: Glenloch Tea Museum

body: I visited the tea museum as part of a day-long 'tea'athon (also visiting plantations and a factory). As a stand-alone attraction, I was left rather confused as to exactly how tea was processed. However I did quite enjoy the visit and found some of the exhibits laugh out loud funny, such as the 'origional wooden plank' and the heap of 'origional telephone wires'; It is housed in a large beautiful old tea factory, which they have struggled to fill the space. It was well worth visiting an actual working tea factory later that day as it cleared up any unanswered question I had about tea production.
title: Kind of in-tea-resting

body: If you are not too pressed for time this is worth the visit. It is what I expected, but interesting just the same.
title: Interesting and worth a visit

body: I didn't find any of the touristic gifts and souvenirs particularly cheap in Sri Lanka, but the tea at this place, while not exactly cheap, was really good value for money compared to everywhere else and to prices back home. I bought dozens of boxes of tea for myself and as souvenirs to take home. The best packaging and presentation of all the teas I saw!
title: Stock up on tea

body: Good to learn about tea but if you want the best experience visit a local tea factory.But you can learn about the history of famous ceylon tea.
title: Learnt a bit of tea.

body: we had to hire a tuk tuk from the city as it is located in a mountain close to kandy.you could also visit a tea factory on your way to nuweraeliya.the climate changes when you are there and the staff are very friendly. call them up first to check with the timings and then go as they have odd opened hours.
title: very far but worth it

body: Try visiting a functioning tea factory instead, you can see how things work. The museum is just a big space with nothing in it.
title: Not Worth Taking the Detour
Worth a drive up
body: Lovely museum, knowledgable staff, reasonable entrance 500 rs with a cup of tea included.restored and kept beautifully.get a tuk tuk drive up

title: Not for the faint hearted!
body: The tea museum was very interesting - it was a lovely view looking at the tea pickers and the fields - however the journey was quite hairy and long (hairpin bends up and down the mountain for a number of hours)

title: srilankan tea
body: being a exporting country for tea, we can get best tastes of the national tea live

title: Make a hot cup
body: Been to couple of tea museum..not much different may be the first timer will love it..

title: An experience
body: it was interesting to see the different stages to how tea is dried and made. the tea however is very strong. Good experience.

title: Tea up your life!
body: So you have been to the Temple, the botanical gardens, Pinnewella and yet a day to kill in Kandy and like tea like I do. Why not visit the Tea Museum in Hantana, just a 15 mnts ride away from the Kandy city centre.The building with it's 4 stories dates back to 1925. Most of the machinery is found on the ground floor and the audio visuals and the library are on the 2nd.You can take a three wheeler from the city centre, but will have to walk back a short distance to catch one back to Kandy. (Closed on Mondays - April 2012)

title: cup for two.
body: interesting place to visit and learn about the production of tea making but not a good place for those with breathing problems such as asthma or allergies as the smell of tea can get to you.

title: This is the authentic Tea Museum
body: There are a lot of tourist "tea factories" in Kandy and nearby regions, those are only to give quick explanations, and sell very expensive tea. I recommend better to visit the Tea Museum, a real museum with all the Victorian machinery, in an original building. The explanation is very good!
